contributions: Introduces modularity as a quality function for community partitions, ranging from -0.5 to 1 with values above 0.3 indicating meaningful structure
Describes the Girvan-Newman divisive hierarchical algorithm using edge betweenness centrality with O(m^2 n) time complexity
Presents the Louvain algorithm as a scalable greedy modularity optimizer running in O(m log n) time
Explains the BigCLAM generative model for overlapping communities using non-negative matrix factorization
Documents the resolution limit of modularity-based methods, which cannot reliably detect communities smaller than approximately sqrt(m) edges
limitations: Girvan-Newman has O(m^2 n) time complexity, making it infeasible for graphs with millions of nodes

Louvain has a fundamental resolution limit: it cannot reliably detect communities smaller than approximately sqrt(m) edges due to a property of the modularity function itself (proven by Fortunato and Barthélemy, 2007)
Modularity maximization is NP-hard in general
BigCLAM optimization is non-convex, and selecting the number of communities K requires model selection
Partition-based methods systematically misclassify boundary nodes that sit at the intersection of multiple communities
methods: The chapter covers three main algorithmic approaches. The Girvan-Newman algorithm (2002) iteratively removes edges with highest betweenness centrality to produce a hierarchical dendrogram, then cuts at the modularity-maximizing level. The Louvain algorithm (Blondel et al., 2008) uses a greedy two-phase strategy: Phase 1 locally optimizes modularity by moving nodes to neighboring communities based on incremental delta-Q calculations, and Phase 2 compresses discovered communities into super-nodes, repeating until convergence. BigCLAM (Yang and Leskovec, 2013) is a generative model where edge probability between nodes u and v is P(A_uv=1) = 1 - exp(-F_u · F_v), fitted via coordinate ascent maximization of a log-likelihood objective over non-negative membership vectors.
results: On the Zachary Karate Club graph (34 nodes, 78 edges), the correct ground-truth partition achieves modularity Q ≈ 0.37. Girvan-Newman correctly identifies the two factions by first removing the bridge edge between the instructor's and administrator's clusters. The Karate Club is used as the primary benchmark throughout. Modularity interpretation: Q < 0 indicates anti-community structure, 0 ≤ Q < 0.3 is weak/no structure, 0.3 ≤ Q < 0.7 is moderate to strong structure, and Q ≥ 0.7 is very strong (rare in practice). Louvain's resolution limit prevents detecting communities smaller than ~sqrt(m) edges—for a 10M-edge network, communities with fewer than ~3,162 edges may be missed.
tldr: This chapter covers community detection algorithms—including Louvain, Girvan-Newman, and BigCLAM—and their applications to social and fraud networks, emphasizing that real networks organize into dense clusters of internally connected nodes sparsely linked to the rest of the graph.
